Bernardo O'Higgins. The Chilean military leader and statesman who, working alongside José de San Martín, liberated Chile from Spanish colonial rule and served as the nation's first supreme director. He is revered as the founder of the Chilean republic.

O'Higgins was the son of an Irish-born Spanish official and a Chilean creole, raised in Spain before returning to South America to join the independence movement. He commanded Chilean forces alongside San Martín during the crossing of the Andes in 1817 and the decisive Battle of Maipú in 1818. After Chile won its independence, O'Higgins served as Supreme Director from 1818 to 1823, establishing the legal and institutional foundations of the Chilean state. He implemented land redistribution, weakened the Catholic Church's political influence, and abolished aristocratic titles to promote republicanism. When internal political opposition mounted, he exiled himself to Peru in 1823, as Chile's rulers rejected his more radical reforms. Despite not achieving all his goals, O'Higgins remains a revered figure in Chilean history, honored as the Father of Chile.
